title: Rate Limiter Advanced
description: Master sliding window algorithms, per-user API tiers, distributed rate limiting across regions, graceful degradation, and proper X-RateLimit header implementation.

segments.text: Fixed window rate limiting has a fatal flaw: boundary bursting. If your limit is one hundred requests per minute and a user sends one hundred at 11:59:59 and another hundred at 12:00:01, they've sent two hundred in two seconds. The sliding window algorithms fix this, but each has different memory and accuracy trade-offs.

The sliding window log stores every request timestamp. To check: remove timestamps older than the window, count remaining. If under the limit, allow. Perfectly accurate but expensive — at a thousand requests per second, you're storing a thousand timestamps per user. Redis sorted sets work well but memory adds up at scale.

The sliding window counter is the sweet spot. Track counts for the current and previous fixed windows. Estimate the sliding window count as: previous window count times overlap percentage plus current window count. Cloudflare uses this approach — it's ninety-nine point seven percent accurate with constant memory per user.

Real rate limiters have tiered limits. Stripe's API: test mode gets twenty-five requests per second, basic production gets one hundred, enterprise gets thousands with custom negotiation. Implement with a tier lookup table and per-API-key counters. The API key maps to a tier, the tier defines limits per endpoint.

Distributed rate limiting across regions is hard. If your limit is one hundred requests per second globally, and you have three regions, each region can't independently allow one hundred. Options: centralized counter in one region adds latency. Local counters with gossip synchronization allow temporary over-limit. Stripe uses a central Redis cluster with local caches.

A user's rate limit is one thousand per minute globally. They're sending five hundred from US-East and five hundred from EU-West simultaneously. With eventually-consistent local counters, both regions might allow the full five hundred, resulting in one thousand total. Is this acceptable?
segments.thought_prompt: How much over-limit tolerance is acceptable in distributed rate limiting? What factors drive this decision?

segments.text: When a user hits the rate limit, return 429 Too Many Requests with a Retry-After header. But for critical operations, consider queuing instead of rejecting. GitHub's API queues requests that slightly exceed limits and processes them with a small delay — better than a hard rejection for a CI/CD pipeline mid-deployment.

X-RateLimit headers tell clients their status. X-RateLimit-Limit: the maximum allowed. X-RateLimit-Remaining: how many left. X-RateLimit-Reset: Unix timestamp when the window resets. Smart clients use these to self-throttle before hitting the limit. This reduces server load and improves the developer experience significantly.

Race conditions are the hidden danger. Two concurrent requests check the counter, both see ninety-nine out of one hundred, both increment to one hundred, both are allowed. Use Redis MULTI/EXEC for atomic check-and-increment, or Lua scripts for complex logic. Never separate the read and write into two operations.
Design a rate limiter for an API gateway handling fifty thousand requests per second across three geographic regions, supporting per-user tiered limits with sub-millisecond overhead per request.
segments.thought_prompt: Design a distributed rate limiter for 50K req/s across 3 regions with sub-ms overhead.

segments.text: Advanced rate limiting uses sliding window counters for accuracy with constant memory, tiered limits per API key, distributed counters with acceptable over-limit tolerance, and proper response headers for client self-throttling. The Staff-level insight: rate limiting is as much a product decision as a technical one — define what 'too many' means for each user tier and each endpoint.
